source.author: hor
source.text: Debes hoc etiam rescribere, sit tibi curae quantae conveniat Munatius; an male sarta gratia nequiquam coit et rescinditur?
source.text_original: Debes hoc etiam rescribere, sit tibi curae  / quantae conveniat Munatius; an male sarta / gratia nequiquam coit et rescinditur?
source.text_english: You should also write back on this point: take care how great a burden Munatius is suited to; or is friendship, badly mended, joined together and torn apart to no purpose?

reuse.author: hier
reuse.text: Unde et Tullius in Commentariis causarum pro Gabinio: Ego, inquit, cum omnes amicitias tuendas semper putavi summa religione et fide, tum eas maxime quae essent ex inimicitiis revocatae in gratiam: propterea quod integris amicitiis officium praetermissum, imprudentiae, vel ut gravius interpretemur negligentiae excusatione defenditur; post reditum in gratiam, si quid est commissum, id non neglectum, sed violatum putatur: nec imprudentiae, sed perfidiae assignari solet. Flaccus Horatius quoque in Epistola quam scribit ad Florum: Male, ait, sarta Gratia nequidquam coit, et rescinditur.
reuse.text_original: Unde et Tullius in Commentariis causarum pro Gabinio: «Ego, inquit, cum omnes amicitias tuendas semper putavi summa religione et fide, tum eas maxime quae essent ex inimicitiis revocatae in gratiam: propterea quod integris amicitiis officium praetermissum, imprudentiae, vel (ut gravius interpretemur) negligentiae excusatione defenditur; post reditum in gratiam, si quid est commissum, id non neglectum, sed violatum putatur: nec imprudentiae, sed perfidiae assignari solet.» Flaccus Horatius quoque in Epistola quam scribit ad Florum: Male, ait, sarta Gratia nequidquam coit, et rescinditur.
reuse.text_english: Whence Tullius too, in the Commentaries on the case for Gabinius, says: I, he says, have always thought that all friendships should be maintained with the utmost reverence and good faith, but especially those which have been restored from enmity to harmony, because in intact friendships an omitted duty is defended by the excuse of thoughtlessness, or, if we interpret more strictly, of negligence; after a reconciliation, if anything has been committed, it is thought not to have been neglected but violated, and it is usually attributed not to thoughtlessness but to treachery. Horace Flaccus also, in the Epistle which he writes to Florus, says: Poorly does patched-up favor come together to no purpose, and is torn apart.
